newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: FEATURE - Cash-strapped Zimbabwe to host solar summit.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cash-strapped Zimbabwe to host solar summit.

text.p: Cash-strapped Zimbabwe will host a summit on solar energy this month which organisers hope will help to spread light to some of the many millions now without electricity worldwide.

Under a blazing African summer sun, Harare -- sold by tourism promoters as Africa's Sunshine City -- will play host to political leaders and experts discussing greater use of power from the sun's rays, wind and other renewable sources of energy.

The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO), which is co-hosting the Zimbabwe conference, says it is determined to boost solar use under a 1996-2005 World Solar Programme because, even with greater use of oil, at least 30 percent of the world population might be condemned to a life without electricity.
It says, for example, some villages in the Third World are simply too remote to be linked into any national electricity grids burning fossil fuels like oil.

Some 300 solar energy projects are due to be launched at the Harare conference, which is also expected to be attended by U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, South African President Nelson Mandela, Iranian President Rafsanjani and delegates from some oil-producing countries, such as Saudi Arabia.

For Zimbabwe, the meeting is proving a financial challenge. With less than two weeks to go to the World Solar Summit, the southern African state says it has raised less than 10 percent of the Z$95 million (U.S.$9.3 million) it estimates the conference will cost.

"The situation is rather desperate...but we are hopeful the money will flow in and that we will get what we need," says Rose Peters, vice-chairman of a national fund-raising committee that President Robert Mugabe set up to carry the begging bowl to the local business community and Harare-based diplomatic missions.

Mugabe's government -- which is under pressure from key international donors to cut sharply a budget deficit that hit 10.1 percent in the last financial year -- says it doesn't have the required money.

So far, small donations have come from Zimbabwean companies and a couple of countries, indicating, according to some local analysts, that the world does not share the hope that the World Solar Summit would leave the Third World's 2.4 billion who live without electricity closer to light and energy from solar power.
Zimbabwean vice-president Simon Muzenda says only 25 heads of state have confirmed they will attend the September 16-17 summit, which organisers initially expected to attract up to 80 leaders.

But Muzenda recently said that many more might still turn up, and his government's organising committee was still asking ordinary Zimbabweans with good houses and cars to rent them out for reasonable rates to enable it to accommodate delegates.
Many of Harare's hotels are fully booked and organisers say some of the expected 3,000 delegates to the World Solar Summit must be accommodated in private homes.

Fund-raising celebrity dinners and special television and radio programmes have been lined up to drum up public support for the conference, which Muzenda and other Zimbabwean officials say will set the world onto a solid path to provide light and energy for those struggling without.
"This is a conference that will change the face of the world. It will have an impact greater than your contribution," said Peter Pamire, chairman of the national fund-raising committee.
Local firms, choking on high interest rates, say they are trying their best to help but are finding it hard to give big donations.
